electric-charges-fields: Choose a closed coaxial cylinder of radius r and length L around an effectively infinite, uniformly charged line. The field is radial and constant on the curved side; end-cap flux is zero.
Cancel L to obtain the field magnitude. Its direction is outward for positive line charge and inward for negative charge.
potential-capacitance: Take two large plates of area A, separation d and charges ±Q. Neglect fringing; between the plates the fields of the two sheets add.
The potential difference is field times separation. Substitute it into the definition of capacitance.
If a dielectric completely fills the gap, replace vacuum permittivity by its dielectric value.
current-electricity: In the simple Drude model, an electron's mean drift-speed magnitude depends on the mean time τ between collisions.
Use carrier density n, cross-section A and the approximately uniform field along length L.
Combine the equations, then compare with Ohm’s law to read off resistance and resistivity.
moving-charges-magnetism: Choose a circular Amperian path of radius r around an effectively infinite, straight wire. By symmetry, the magnetic field is tangent to the circle and has constant magnitude.
Solve for B; use the right-hand grip rule for its direction.
magnetism-matter: For a small current loop in a uniform field, opposite forces make a couple: net force is zero, but torque is not. For one turn:
For N turns, define magnetic dipole moment and write the resulting aligning torque.
electromagnetic-induction: A straight conducting rod of length ℓ moves perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field. Charges feel a magnetic force until the electric force from separation balances it.
Multiply the field by the rod length to find the magnitude of the induced end-to-end emf. A current needs a closed circuit.
alternating-current: Take the series-circuit current as phase reference. Resistor voltage is in phase; inductor voltage leads and capacitor voltage lags by 90°. Thus the reactive voltages subtract as phasors.
Divide by the current to obtain the impedance. At resonance the reactances cancel.
electromagnetic-waves: Two surfaces can share the same boundary loop: one cuts a charging wire and the other bulges between capacitor plates. The latter encloses no conduction current, so Ampère’s original law alone gives conflicting answers.
For ideal plates, electric flux is proportional to the charge. Hence the displacement current between the plates equals the wire current.
